newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries narrowly mixed as data awaited.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries narrowly mixed as data awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury securities prices ended narrowly mixed on Monday after remarks on a newswire in which Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillips hinted no immediate need for a tightening existed.

Players remained nervous ahead of Wednesday's retail sales report, however. Sales were expected to rise 0.7 percent -- 0.5 percent excluding automobiles -- on Wednesday, but a surprising number could jolt the market, economists said. While a number of economic releases were expected, retail sales were seen as being the primary release of the week.
The yield on the 30-year bond rose to 6.69 percent at one point in the trading session, the highest since the closing level on July 2.
Fred Sturm, economist at Fuji Securities, said investors didn't like the bond market on Friday when it fell sharply and that sentiment only changed after remarks by Phillips.

"Retail sales and producer prices have been largely friendly to the bond market. That's going to change," Sturm said. Consumer spending was likely to be hefty in the second half of the year, he said, as it has outpaced the first half in five of the last seven years.
Headline PPI has fallen 1.7 percent this year, Sturm said, "and the question you have to ask is what are the prospects for getting that back."
He said commodity prices had rebounded since mid-year.
"All of the good news is behind us," Sturm said.
"We saw a nice reversal. The market's sort of betwixt and between right now," said Cary Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics.
Leahey said there was a lot of worry that retail sales could come in stronger than expected and could react adversely if unit labor costs come in strong on Tuesday.

"Phillips' comments were determined by the market to be bullish," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. They laid to rest the notion that the Federal Reserve would further tighten monetary policy anytime in the near future, she said.

"I still think we need to be a little bit cautious, there could be some bad news coming," Dennis said. "The economy is strong, so lingering prospects (of strong growth) are still out there," Dennis said.
She said strong retail sales data could undermine market psychology.
The Treasury's 30-year issue was ending up 3/32 at 96-23/32 to yield 6.63 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, three-month bills were one basis point higher at 5.16 percent. Six-month bills were up two basis points at 5.25 percent and year bills were up two basis points at 5.29 percent.
The 10-year issue was 3/32 higher at 98-10 to yield 6.36 percent. The five-year was 4/32 higher at 99-6/32 to yield 6.19 percent and the two-year 3/32 higher to yield 5.96 percent.
